title: With help from data, art museums are reframing the visitor experience
gist: A multi-year study at Amsterdam's Van Gogh Museum used digital-guide interaction data to build a predictive model of visitor movement (63-96% accuracy across tasks), showing museums can measurably steer foot traffic and engagement through layout and recommendation design, while curators debate whether AI-driven personalization should challenge visitor taste or just predict and reinforce it.

insights.claim: Researchers from MIT Sloan, Georgia Tech, and IESE Business School built a "pathway multinomial logit" (pathway MNL) model using digital-guide interaction data from 25,000 of 1.5 million visits to Amsterdam's Van Gogh Museum (2019-2021) to predict visitor movement decisions and identify artwork placements that maximize the expected number of pieces seen.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A validated statistical model for predicting museum-visitor pathways gives cultural institutions (and adjacent physical-digital venues) a concrete analytics tool for layout and engagement optimization.
insights.locator: According to the authors, a visitor’s next move

insights.claim: The pathway MNL model achieved 63 percent accuracy predicting the specific next artwork a visitor transitions to, 81 percent accuracy predicting whether a visitor reaches a given piece at all, and 96 percent accuracy predicting when a visitor will leave the museum.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: These are concrete, testable benchmark accuracy figures for anyone evaluating or building similar visitor-behavior prediction models in museums or comparable experiential venues.
insights.locator: The model was also used to predict visitors’ likelihood

insights.claim: Because physically rearranging a permanent collection is costly and constrained, the researchers instead used simulation rather than real-world reshuffling to test layout changes, finding that moving popular art away from "leaky" transit spots like stairwells and strategically swapping pieces could increase both the number of artworks seen and time spent, without needing physical experimentation.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A simulation-first approach to layout testing lets museums (and similarly constrained physical-retail spaces) de-risk layout changes before committing to costly physical moves.
insights.locator: Rather than actually moving pieces, the researchers used a simulation

insights.claim: Multimedia guide users largely followed the app's suggested viewing order, and even subtle changes to the ordering of recommendations on the digital guide measurably shifted physical foot-traffic patterns through the museum, according to product manager Lisa van den Bos: "We actually have a lot of power in how we move people through."
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The digital guide interface functions as a real-time behavioral lever over physical crowd flow, meaning software-level recommendation changes can directly reshape in-person visitor movement without any physical renovation.
insights.quote: We actually have a lot of power in how we move people through
insights.locator: Multimedia guide users largely visited recommended artworks

insights.claim: Counterintuitively, increased crowding around an artwork, up to a certain point, increased visitor engagement with nearby unrelated works — likely because congestion itself signals perceived quality — per researcher Abhishek Deshmane: "When there are more people... people are more likely to go and view artworks that they probably wouldn't have seen."
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: This overturns the assumption that congestion is purely a negative for engagement metrics, implying museums (or any crowded venue) could deliberately use crowding signals to boost secondary-item exposure rather than only trying to minimize it.
insights.quote: When there are more people, at least up to a certain number…people are more likely to go and view artworks that they probably wouldn’t have seen
insights.locator: Perhaps surprisingly, the data revealed that congestion

themes.theme: Underused data and low guide adoption

insights.claim: Despite years of accumulating rich digital-guide interaction data, most museums "almost never" actually review or use that data for decision-making, according to Tapart's Sietze de Jong, who called it a "gold mine" — sector-wide digital-guide uptake for paid tours is typically only about 10 percent, versus the Van Gogh Museum's 36 percent average daily bookings in 2023.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Widespread under-utilization of already-collected visitor data, combined with low baseline guide adoption industry-wide, means most museums are sitting on unmonetized analytics value that a data/analytics vendor could capture.
insights.quote: Every museum requests us to do analytics and include it in their audio guide… but when we ask them if they reviewed the data, they almost never have
insights.locator: Museums rarely use digital guide data

themes.theme: AI expansion and its boundaries in museums

insights.claim: Museums are expanding AI/ML use beyond layout optimization — analyzing visitor records and collections databases and generating automated textual artwork descriptions from collection data — but are explicitly staying away from conversational or generative AI playing a curatorial role or "speaking as" artists, due to concerns about accuracy and artistic integrity.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A clear, self-imposed boundary (analytics/description AI yes, generative curatorial-voice AI no) marks where museum-sector AI adoption is likely to concentrate near-term, relevant for AI-in-culture vendors scoping product fit.
insights.locator: Some applications seem less likely to see widespread adoption soon

insights.claim: MUNCH's "New Snow" exhibition (2024-2025) used AI/ML to match visitor-submitted drawings to the closest corresponding Edvard Munch sketch, generating over 70,000 visitor drawings and creating an interactive engagement channel for fragile works that are rarely displayed physically due to their fragility.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified case (70,000+ submissions) of AI enabling public interaction with otherwise-inaccessible fragile collection items demonstrates a working commercial/engagement use case for AI in museums.
insights.locator: MUNCH’s New Snow exhibition, available in two waves

insights.claim: Curators interviewed argue institutions should deliberately design recommendations to challenge visitor taste rather than simply predict and reinforce existing preferences, warning that pure preference-optimization risks "reinforcing the canon" of already-famous works and turning museums into what one called "optimization machines" that undermine their educational mission.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: This tension between engagement-maximizing personalization and the stated educational/curatorial mission is a governance risk for any institution adopting recommendation algorithms, with reputational stakes if critics see it as reducing culture to engagement metrics.
insights.quote: Showing people artworks that you think they’re going to like actually is a disservice
insights.locator: While the answer is not straightforward

insights.claim: The pathway MNL researchers argue their modeling approach generalizes beyond museums to any "sequential experience that blends the physical and digital," explicitly naming entertainment, education, and retail as other applicable domains for the same visitor/customer-pathway analytics technique.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: If the technique transfers as claimed, it points to a broader addressable market for physical-digital pathway analytics vendors beyond museums, including theme parks, retail stores, and stadiums.
insights.locator: Beyond museums, they feel their approach has direct application

insights.claim: A 2023 McKinsey & Company report found museums are grounding longer-term strategic decisions more in data, partly driven by rising expectations from trustees, funders, and governments rather than purely visitor-experience motives.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: External stakeholder pressure (funders, governments), not just visitor experience, is identified as a driver of data adoption — relevant to forecasting how fast museums will keep investing in analytics regardless of proven visitor-side ROI.
insights.locator: Museums also seek to ground longer-term strategic decisions

insights.claim: In 2025 the Van Gogh Museum replaced its multimedia guide hardware and software (moving to Samsung hardware and NOUS Digital software), with the redesign directly informed by the research team's findings on visitor behavior — a concrete case of the academic study translating into an actual vendor and technology purchasing decision.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A named vendor swap driven by this research is direct evidence that behavioral-analytics findings can convert into real procurement decisions, relevant to vendors like Samsung and NOUS Digital competing for museum technology contracts.
insights.locator: In 2025, the VGM announced a redesigned version
